source.title: LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately
source.authors: Jia-Chen Zhao; Jing Huang; Zheng-Xuan Wu; David Bau; Wei-Yan Shi

page_placements.theme: Where the direction acts: template positions, layers, pathways and upstream features

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own measurements and interventions that distinguish a harmfulness direction from refusal signals, refining how refusal-direction findings should be interpreted. It does not reproduce the original direction-ablation experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper measures harmfulness and refusal representations, steers both directions, and analyzes jailbreak prompts. Table 1's post-instruction-token comparison is not a direction intervention; it is noted under fits_no_version. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study steers a tpost-inst difference-in-means refusal direction (V1 addition) and compares it causally with a separate tinst harmfulness direction. This argues that refusal and harmfulness judgment are encoded separately (V5). It also measures refusal-cluster signals under jailbreaks (V3). It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add the authors' central causal claim: steering along the refusal direction reinforces refusal without reversing the harmfulness judgment. Also add that they propose a Latent Guard built on the harmfulness belief, comparable to Llama Guard 3 and robust to the tested fine-tuning attack.
record.recipe_differences: The study extracts a harmfulness difference-in-means direction at tinst and a separate refusal direction at tpost-inst, then uses activation addition and reply inversion. It does not ablate a refusal direction from every layer and position or test retained general capability.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects depend on model, layer, token position, direction, and—in reply inversion—prompt template. The paper reports that models sometimes ignore an inversion question and uses different templates for different models.

fits_no_version.finding: A tinst harmfulness difference-in-means direction also induces refusal when added: 94% on Llama3 at layer 9, weaker on Llama2/Qwen2. Its cosine similarity with the refusal direction is about 0.1 on Llama2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A harmfulness direction distinct from the refusal direction can also causally induce refusal, less reliably.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing post-instruction template tokens lowers refusal of harmful prompts: from 100/96/98% to 85.3/58.9/81.3%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal depends strongly on post-instruction template tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmfulness directions differ by risk category (e.g. average cosine 0.6), while refusal directions are similar across categories (0.89).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmfulness representations are category-specific; refusal representations are shared across categories.

fits_no_version.finding: Δharmful is almost unchanged after acceptance fine-tuning on 50–400 examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow acceptance fine-tuning leaves the latent harmfulness representation intact.

record.peer_reviewed: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)
record.problems: The study focuses on open models of 7B and 8B and says generalization to larger models is unclear. It describes itself as an existence proof rather than an exhaustive account, does not study the role of individual layers, and uses several figure-only results without reported uncertainty. It does not test general capability retention after ablation.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-bearing results were left out. Table 1's post-instruction-token removal results do not intervene on the claimed direction, so they are summarized under fits_no_version rather than recorded as direction-ablation rows. Cited results from prior work were excluded.

untested.parts: Directional ablation removing refusal, and retention of general capabilities. Only addition of the direction is tested.
All parts: no weight-edit abliteration is tested.
Causal suppression of the direction by attacks, and adversarial training against ablation.
All parts: multi-dimensional, cone or affine accounts of refusal itself are not tested.
All parts: directions are not transferred across languages, variants or training stages.
All parts: the existence of a single direction is not varied with training.
All parts: no reasoning models are tested.

missing.what: Reply-inversion results on Llama3-8B, and on Qwen2 with two other templates, reported as consistent
Cosine similarity of about 0.1 between harmfulness and refusal directions on Llama2 (held-out refused 0.57 vs accepted -0.14)
Refusal direction applied to instruction tokens only has near-zero effect in reply inversion
Position sweep: the direction extracted at tinst gives the strongest harmfulness flip; clustering by harmfulness appears only at tinst

record.verdict_notes: Rows R19–R21 and R22–R23 lack an identified model. The V1 evidence is addition only; there are no ablation or capability tests. The harmfulness direction is not the V1 direction, so its steering rows were moved off V1.

versions.untested_parts: It tests adding the harmfulness difference-in-means direction for refusal effects, but not ablating it from every layer and position, compliance after ablation, or preservation of general capabilities.
No weight-edit ablation or released-model abliteration is evaluated.
The study measures harmfulness and refusal beliefs under jailbreak prompts, but does not causally test suppression of the refusal direction or train a defense against its ablation.
It distinguishes harmfulness from refusal directions, but does not test whether refusal itself is affine, conical, or carried by multiple refusal directions.
The study tests separation using representations, steering, and an inversion task; it does not establish a complete account of all harmfulness judgments or refusal decisions.
It tests separate models with model-specific analyses, not transfer of a direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages.
It evaluates one adversarial fine-tuning setup, but does not test whether training choices determine whether a single removable refusal direction exists.

statements.correction: 2507.11878, Section 4 and Figure 6 (model not named): GCG-suffix and template jailbreaks generally give negative Δrefuse (cluster-cosine score at tpost-inst, not a direction projection). Figure only; correlational.
statements.problem: R20/R21 are cited for 'lower the projection onto it'. This study does not measure a projection. Its measure, Δrefuse, is a layer-averaged difference in cosine similarity to cluster centres at tpost-inst. The text gives no numbers, and the Figure 6 model is not named.

statements.correction: 2507.11878, Section 4 and Figure 6 (model not named): in some cases, persuasion makes the model read the prompt as harmless (negative Δharmful). Persuasion's Δrefuse is not stated. The other jailbreaks generally give negative Δrefuse.
statements.problem: R19 is cited for 'attacks succeed without suppressing the direction'. The text does not say this for persuasion. It says only that persuasion sometimes makes Δharmful negative, and it gives no Δrefuse for persuasion. The record labels R19 limits_scope, not challenges.

statements.correction: tinst: clustering by harmfulness across all layers in all three models. tpost-inst (last token of the sequence): clustering by refusal, from early layers in Llama3 and Qwen2 but only in later layers in Llama2. Section 3.2, Figure 2; figure only.
statements.problem: 'By refusal at post-instruction tokens ... across layers' overstates. tpost-inst is only the last post-instruction token; Appendix F tests other positions. In Llama2 the tpost-inst refusal clustering appears only in later layers.

statements.correction: Qwen2 reply inversion (Figure 5): the harmfulness direction flips harmless 'No' to 'Certainly'. The reverse harmfulness direction flips harmful prompts to 'No'. The refusal direction keeps 'No', the reverse refusal direction gives 'Certainly' on harmless prompts, and it fails to flip harmful prompts. Results are consistent on Llama3 (Figure 12) and with two more templates (Figure 11). Ordinary prompting: the harmfulness direction elicits 94% refusal (Llama3, layer 9).
statements.problem: For this study, 'a harm direction moves the harm judgment without refusal' is wrong under ordinary prompting: adding the harmfulness direction itself elicits refusal. Also, reverse refusal-direction steering on harmless prompts does flip the answer to 'Certainly'; the authors read this as a surface acceptance cue.

statements.correction: Appendix E.2: templates were adapted per model because some models sometimes answered the instruction instead of the inversion question. Results were similar with two more templates on Qwen2 (Figure 11) and on Llama3 (Figure 12). Appendix E.1: the refusal direction was applied to all tokens and the harmfulness direction to tokens before the inversion question. Applied to instruction tokens only, the refusal direction had minimal effect (Figure 10, Qwen2).
statements.problem: The facts are mostly right. But the text does not show that the results depend on these choices: the separation held across templates and models. Models ignored the inversion question only 'in some cases'.

statements.correction: Context for 2507.11878: Table 1 shows refusal of AdvBench harmful prompts falling without post-instruction tokens to 85.3/58.9/81.3% (Llama2/Llama3/Qwen2; substring scoring; coherence not measured). Figure 19 shows two coherent, compliant Llama2 outputs.
Add: per Appendix E.2, results were consistent across the three Qwen2 templates and on Llama3.

Persuasion: negative Δharmful in some cases (Figure 6, model not named). Llama2: Δharmful stays positive for many accepted harmful examples. tpost-inst refusal clustering: early layers in Llama3/Qwen2, later layers in Llama2. Reply-inversion results consistent across templates (Figure 11) and on Llama3 (Figure 12).
statements.problem: Three overstatements. Persuasion flips the harm judgment only 'in some cases'. Accepted harmful prompts read as harmful 'for many examples', not all. Refusal clustering at tpost-inst appears only in later layers for Llama2. Also, 'templates adapted per model' is a method caveat; the results were consistent across templates.
